title: The CAP Theorem: Pick Two, You Can't Have Three
subtitle: Spread data across many machines and physics forces a brutal choice: when the network splits, do you stay consistent or stay available? You can't do both.
hook: Once your data lives on more than one machine, a hard truth kicks in — proven, not opinion. When the network between your machines hiccups (and it *will*), you must choose: keep answering requests but risk serving different answers, or refuse to answer to stay perfectly correct. You cannot have both. This is the **CAP theorem**, and it quietly shapes every large system on Earth. Today: the trade-off you can't escape.

sections.heading: The three letters
sections.body:
CAP names three things a distributed data store might want:
- **C — Consistency**: every read sees the latest write (all machines agree).
- **A — Availability**: every request gets an answer, no errors.
- **P — Partition tolerance**: it keeps working even when the network between machines breaks.

The theorem: when a **partition** happens (machines can't talk), you can guarantee **C or A, but not both.** And since network failures are inevitable at scale, P isn't optional — so the real, live choice is always **C vs. A**.

sections.caption: When the network splits, you're forced to choose: refuse answers to stay consistent (CP), or keep answering and risk staleness (AP).

sections.label: The choice depends on the job
sections.body: A bank ledger picks **consistency** — better to reject a transaction than double-spend (CP). A social feed picks **availability** — better to show a slightly stale like-count than an error page (AP). Neither is 'right'; the correct answer depends on what breaks worse for your users: a wrong answer, or no answer. Great system design is knowing which side of CAP each part of your product wants.

sections.label: The nuance nobody tells you
sections.body: CAP is a simplification — the choice isn't all-or-nothing. Modern systems tune it per-operation and add 'eventual consistency' (answer now, reconcile a moment later). But the core lesson holds: at scale, correctness and availability trade against each other whenever the network misbehaves, and pretending otherwise is how outages happen.

sections.caption: The CAP theorem — consistency vs. availability, explained.

takeaways: **CAP**: Consistency, Availability, Partition-tolerance — a distributed store can't guarantee all three.
Network **partitions** are inevitable at scale, so P is a must — the live choice is **C vs. A**.
**CP** (banks): refuse rather than serve wrong data. **AP** (feeds): stay up, tolerate staleness.
Neither is universally right — it depends on whether a *wrong* answer or *no* answer hurts more.
Reality is tunable (per-operation, 'eventual consistency'), but the core trade-off is real.

quiz.q: During a network partition, CAP says you must choose between…
quiz.explain: Partitions are unavoidable, so it's C vs. A — you can't keep both.

quiz.q: A bank ledger should lean which way?
options: AP — stay available, tolerate stale/wrong balances
CP — stay consistent, refuse rather than risk double-spend
quiz.explain: For money, a wrong answer is worse than no answer — choose consistency.

quiz.q: CALLBACK: Why is 'partition tolerance' non-negotiable — and which earlier lesson explains why networks split?
options: Networks are packet-switched and can drop/reroute (Day 6) — links fail, so machines will sometimes be unable to talk
quiz.explain: From the networking lesson: the internet is unreliable by design. Since partitions WILL happen, you must plan for them — leaving the real choice as C vs. A.

tg_quiz.q: When a distributed system's network splits, CAP forces a choice between…
tg_quiz.correct: Right — C vs A. You can't keep both during a partition.
tg_quiz.wrong: It's Consistency vs Availability — partitions force the pick.
tg_quiz.explain: Banks pick C; social feeds pick A.
